summary:
Claude Code 2.1.240 is installed (npm global, 337 MB compiled bin/claude.exe). I read the embedded JS bundle and embedded docs out of the binary, cross-checked https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks, and ran end-to-end probes by pointing the CLI at a local fake Anthropic SSE endpoint (the user's own gateway was returning 521), so no real inference credits were spent and no user config was modified.

CORE CONTRACT (all verified): 31 hook events exist, not 4. Per tool call the order is inputSchema validation -> PreToolUse -> rules/mode pipeline -> PermissionRequest (only when the outcome is ask) -> prompt -> execute -> PostToolUse OR PostToolUseFailure -> PostToolBatch. Hook deny IS honoured in bypassPermissions and beats allow rules, because the resolver (NEw) short-circuits on a hook deny before the mode-grant code (d8S) is ever called. Hook allow is a best-effort grant: user deny and ask rules override it. Crash (exit 1 + garbage stdout), missing script, and timeout all FAIL OPEN — measured, with a marker file proving the tool actually executed. Exit 2 is the only blocking exit code. Default command-hook timeout is 600 seconds (var Z_=600000), not 60. permission_mode is in the PreToolUse payload but genuinely absent on session-lifecycle events.

FIVE THINGS THAT MAKE LEASTGRANT'S CLAIMS WRONG OR NARROW:
1. README's "on Claude Code an ask reaches you in every mode" is false. Under `claude -p` a hook ask becomes a DENY in bypassPermissions, manual, acceptEdits, dontAsk and auto. In dontAsk it becomes a deny by mode even interactively. Safe direction, wrong claim — and it is the sentence used to argue Claude Code is strictly stronger than Codex.
2. hook.ts ATTENDED = ['default','plan','ask'] — 'ask' is not a permission mode, and no payload field reports interactivity, so `permission_mode: "default"` in a headless run reads as "a human approved this". Currently unexploitable only because Claude Code denies headless asks so PostToolUse never fires.
3. LeastGrant registers only PreToolUse/PostToolUse. PostToolUseFailure means every failed call is invisible to learning and leaks a pendingById entry. PermissionRequest — which LeastGrant already uses for Codex — is the unused second veto point that fires exactly where the ask currently dies.
4. tool_name is the resolved internal name after toolAliases, not what the model emitted: the model sends `Task`, the hook sees `Agent`. mine.ts learns 'Task' from transcripts and hook.ts judges 'Agent' live, so subagent-spawn signatures can never match.
5. Core's `Decision = allow|ask|deny` and tool_use_id-keyed Pre/Post pairing are Claude-shaped, and already too narrow for Claude Code itself: there is a fourth verdict (`defer`), a mutation channel (`updatedInput`, which I confirmed rewrites a Bash command wholesale), a turn-halt channel (`continue:false`), and two Claude Code events (PermissionRequest, PostToolBatch) that carry no tool_use_id at all.

Also: managed policy `disableAllHooks: true` switches LeastGrant off entirely with no signal in the payload; `--bare` and `--safe-mode` skip hooks; on Windows a bash-shell hook throws (and therefore silently stops enforcing) if Git Bash is absent. claims.question: 6 - What happens if the hook process CRASHES (non-zero exit, garbage on stdout)? Fail open or fail closed? CRITICAL.

The caller is hooks.(*PreToolHookConverter).applyPreToolHooks (@0x14193a4e0): at 0x14193a873 it invokes the hook, at 0x14193a875 it tests the returned error interface (`test rbx, rbx; jne 0x14193aa25`), and the error branch at 0x14193aa25 does exactly two things - it calls log.ctxlogf with severity 2 (ERROR) and the format string 'pre-tool hook failed: %v' at 0x14193aaba/0x14193aac7, and then at 0x14193aae0 it jumps to 0x14193a80d, which is the LOOP INCREMENT (`mov r10,[rsp+0x78]; inc r10`). It moves on to the next hook and the tool call executes. There is no deny, no abort, no user notification - just a log line the user will never see. Non-zero exit, a crash, a missing interpreter, an unwritable script, and (by the same error path) unparseable stdout all land here identically. This is the single most important fact for LeastGrant on this agent: on Antigravity, killing or breaking the LeastGrant hook silently disables enforcement. claims.question: 9 - Is there a post-execution observation event?
claims.answer: YES - PostToolUse, and it is richer than the docs admit. Docs say the input is stepIdx plus 'error' if the tool failed, and that the output must be an empty JSON object {}. The shipped proto confirms output is genuinely inert (message PostToolHookResult is EMPTY - it is an observation event only, it cannot retroactively veto) but shows the INPUT carries four fields, not two: step_idx, tool_call (the full HookToolCall with name and args), error, and result. There are also two other post-execution-ish events: PostInvocation (fires after tool calls finish, input adds the undocumented model_output and model_thinking, output can inject steps or set terminationBehavior to force_continue/terminate) and Stop (input executionNum, terminationReason, error, fullyIdle, plus undocumented final_model_output; output decision 'continue' blocks termination and re-enters the loop, capped by MaxStopHookContinuations). claims.question: 12 - Anything that would make LeastGrant's enforcement claims for this agent dishonest or overstated.

If the LeastGrant hook exits non-zero, crashes, is deleted, or times out, Antigravity logs 'pre-tool hook failed: %v' to a log nobody reads and RUNS THE TOOL. Any wording like 'LeastGrant enforces on Antigravity' must be qualified: enforcement is best-effort and evaporates on hook failure. This is the opposite of Copilot CLI, which the README already correctly singles out as failing closed. (2) UNRECOGNISED VERDICT == ALLOW. The deny check is a length-4 exact byte compare against 'deny'. A typo, wrong case, a wrapped/nested JSON shape, or an empty stdout is not a deny - it is a pass-through. LeastGrant's Antigravity adapter needs a self-test that asserts a known-bad call is actually blocked, not just that the hook was invoked. (3) 'ask' IS NOT ASK. Mapping LeastGrant's abstract ASK onto Antigravity's 'ask' is the wrong translation: 'ask' respects cached Always-Allow grants and is swallowed by the eager/TURBO auto-execution mode (the disassembly shows 'ask' does not force the prompt register, whereas 'force_ask' does `mov r13d, 1`). The honest mapping is ASK -> force_ask. If LeastGrant ships 'ask', it will silently degrade to allow for exactly the users who most need the prompt. (4) A TIMED-OUT ASK IS A SOFT DENY THAT COACHES EVASION. The prompt timeout message tells the model 'You should proceed as much as possible without access to this resource... Think about alternative ways to achieve your goal (e.g., using different directories...)'. LeastGrant must not describe an unanswered prompt as 'the action was blocked and the agent stopped'. (5) HOOKS ARE BEHIND A REMOTELY-SETTABLE FLAG. CustomizationConfig has an optional bool field enable_json_hooks (field 17). If that config is server-delivered, Google can turn the entire JSON hook system off for a user, and LeastGrant would keep reporting itself as installed while enforcing nothing. LeastGrant should detect and surface hook liveness rather than infer it from the presence of hooks.json. (6) NO MODE VISIBILITY, AND OTHER HOOKS CAN REWRITE YOU. The payload never says which permission mode is active, so LeastGrant cannot honestly claim its decisions are mode-aware. And because hooks are 'merged and executed sequentially' with no documented ordering and PreToolUse can 'overwrite' tool args, another hook (or a malicious .agents/hooks.json committed to a repo the user opened) can mutate a call after LeastGrant reasoned about it. summary:
Google Antigravity is real, shipping, installed here at version 2.11.0 (Electron hub build 2026-08-26, CL 971157550, at %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\antigravity), and it has a fully documented lifecycle-hook API that can gate a tool call before execution. The premise that it might not exist is settled: a well-evidenced YES.

The hook system is inherited from the Windsurf/Cascade ("jetski") codebase and lives in the 153 MB Go agent runtime resources/bin/language_server.exe, not in the VS Code extension host. Google also ships the official hooks documentation on disk as a built-in skill at ~/.gemini/antigravity/builtin/skills/agy-customizations/docs/hooks.md — and that local copy is MORE complete than the public /docs/hooks/ page, which omits the tool-input-rewriting feature.

Model: five events (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PreInvocation, PostInvocation, Stop) plus an undocumented sixth, SessionStart, present in the shipped proto. Config is hooks.json in a customization root: <repo>/.agents/hooks.json or ~/.gemini/config/hooks.json, same shape on every OS. PreToolUse returns five verdicts — allow, deny, ask, force_ask, deny_unless_prior_grant — plus an "overwrite" object that shallow-merges into the tool call's arguments, so a hook can rewrite what executes, not merely veto it.

I could not answer the two most important questions from documentation, because nobody documents them, so I disassembled the binary (Go pclntab + capstone). Results:

- DENY IS REAL AND MODE-INDEPENDENT. applyPreToolHooks byte-compares the decision against "deny" and returns PreToolHookDeniedError during tool-call→step conversion, before the permission manager runs; the permission manager separately short-circuits on reason "hook_deny" before evaluating grants or the auto-execution mode. Deny beats the TURBO/eager preset.
- FAIL OPEN — CRITICAL, AND UNDOCUMENTED. On non-zero exit, crash, unparseable stdout, or the 30 s timeout, the error path logs "pre-tool hook failed: %v" and jumps straight to the loop increment. The tool call runs. Breaking or deleting the LeastGrant hook silently disables enforcement — the exact opposite of Copilot CLI.
- "ask" IS NOT ASK. In the decision switch, force_ask forcibly sets the prompt register (mov r13d, 1) and reaches promptUser; plain "ask" does not, so it defers to cached grants and is swallowed by eager/TURBO. LeastGrant's abstract ASK must map to force_ask.
- A TIMED-OUT PROMPT IS A SOFT DENY that explicitly instructs the model to "think about alternative ways to achieve your goal (e.g., using different directories)".
- The payload exposes no permission mode at all (HookArgsCommon has eight fields, none of them the mode), so a hook cannot adapt to or warn about the active policy.

Caveat on all of it: this is documentation + shipped source + disassembly. I did not run Antigravity, since that needs an interactive desktop session, so nothing here should be labelled probe-verified the way the README labels Claude Code and Copilot.
